Tags: beyond source = added by me, not in his materials.

1. Acute Kidney Injury: Differential and Laboratory Clues

  • Acute kidney injury (AKI) is the broad category: a sudden fall in kidney function. Acute tubular injury/necrosis (ATI/ATN) is only one cause, a specific tubular disease.
  • Dr. Kemp's method: split into big categories first (before, in, after the kidney), then get specific. Clinicians use the same structure on the wards.
Slide: general differential diagnosis for AKI.
CategoryWhere the problem isExamples
Pre-renalStuff not reaching the kidney (low blood flow)Hypoperfusion, shock, dehydration
Renal: glomerularGlomerulusNephritic syndrome (rapidly progressive); nephrotic syndrome is on the slide, but see note
Renal: tubulointerstitialTubules and interstitiumAcute tubular necrosis, acute interstitial nephritis, acute pyelonephritis
Renal: vascularVesselsThrombotic microangiopathy, vasculitis, atheroembolic disease
Post-renalOutflow after the kidneyObstruction: prostatic hyperplasia, stones
His take on nephrotic vs nephriticIn nephrotic syndrome the kidney loses protein but is not otherwise failing, so it is a weak fit for "acute" injury. In nephritic syndrome (and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) there is hypertension, oliguria and real loss of function, so those are the glomerular causes of AKI.
  • Post-renal example: prostatic hyperplasia blocks urine → urine backs up in the bladder → pressure in the kidney → hydronephrosis → failure, which can come on fairly suddenly.

Laboratory testing in AKI

TestWhat it tells you
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)Filtering is the kidney’s job, so reduced GFR = reduced function
BUN and creatinineElevated. The pattern distinguishes pre-renal, renal, post-renal (clinicians cover this in the clinical lecture)
Urinalysis: castsRBC casts → glomerular injury (nephritic, rapidly progressive GN). WBC casts → infection or inflammation (pyelonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis). Tubular cell (epithelial) casts → ATN (also AIN per slide). Granular "muddy brown" casts → ATN
Renal biopsyFor atypical presentations that fit no clinical pattern. Weigh benefit against risk of a long needle in the kidney. Most biopsies he saw in residency were for glomerular disease (minimal change, FSGS, diabetic).

2. Acute Tubular Injury / Necrosis (ATI/ATN)

  • Name: "necrosis" is the older term. Injury is preferred now because tubules can be damaged and not working without visible necrosis. You can diagnose ATN when you see necrosis.
  • Falls under AKI, so: acute decline in function with decreased GFR from injury to tubular epithelial cells; oliguria is possible; granular (muddy) and cellular casts in the urine.

Etiology: two mechanisms

MechanismExamples
IschemiaLow blood flow (shock, hypoperfusion)
NephrotoxicGentamicin, contrast agents, heavy metals, organic solvents, ethylene glycol
Why tubules are vulnerable(1) They need lots of ATP (pumps moving electrolytes), so low oxygen hits them first. (2) Luminal solutes get concentrated as water is reabsorbed, so toxins reach high levels in the tubule.

How the injury lowers GFR

Slide: mechanism. Loss of cell polarity in the proximal tubule means Na⁺ is not reabsorbed, so more Na⁺ reaches the distal tubule, which causes arteriolar vasoconstriction and decreases GFR.
  1. Loss of cell polarity: pumps belong on specific cell surfaces. If they mislocalize, the proximal tubule cannot reabsorb sodium → more sodium delivered to the distal tubule → arteriolar vasoconstriction → ↓ GFR (and potential further ischemia). This is tubuloglomerular feedback. beyond source
  2. Sloughed cells detach → casts that obstruct outflow → ↓ GFR.
  3. Backleak of filtrate through the damaged tubule wall → less urine output.
  4. Ischemic cells recruit inflammatory cells → more tissue injury.

Pathology

Slide: ATN. Yellow arrow = proximal tubule, necrotic (no nuclei). Black arrow = distal tubule, histologically viable.
  • Coagulative necrosis of tubules: the architecture is preserved but the nuclei are gone or pale. Compare a viable tubule (clear nuclei) with a necrotic one (ghost outline).
  • The proximal tubule is the one that dies in the slide; the distal tubule survives.
Slide: ATN at low and high power. Black arrows = necrotic tubules (pale or absent nuclei); yellow arrow = viable tubule.
Slide: dilated proximal tubules with necrotic, flattened, disintegrating epithelium and debris in the lumen. The debris and shed cells become the cellular and muddy brown casts.
Ischemic vs toxicDr. Kemp: pathology cannot usually tell ischemia from a nephrotoxin. You use the history and any special finding (like crystals).

Nephrotoxic example: ethylene glycol (antifreeze)

Slide: ATN from ethylene glycol. Left, H&E with oxalate crystals (arrow). Right, the same crystals under polarized light.
  • Ethylene glycol is not itself harmful to the kidney. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to oxalic acid, which deposits as crystals in the kidney and causes ATN.
  • Crystals are polarizable, which is how pathologists find them.
Slide question22-year-old found unresponsive, fluorescent green-yellow liquid (antifreeze) at the bedside, elevated creatinine, no urine over 12 hours → acute tubular necrosis. Acute pyelonephritis needs fever and WBC casts; chronic pyelonephritis does not present this way; drug-induced interstitial nephritis has no drug history; diffuse cortical necrosis implies a blocked renal artery.

3. Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stones)

  • Nephrolithiasis = kidney stones ("litho" = stone; compare cholelithiasis).
  • Pathogenesis (basic): supersaturation of the urine with a stone component.
  • Risk factors: low fluid intake; diet high in sodium, refined sugars, oxalate, animal protein; grapefruit or apple juice.
  • Epidemiology: by age 70, 11% of men and 5–6% of women have had a stone (more common in men).
Stone type% of stonesNotes
Calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate80%Most common
Struvite (magnesium-ammonium-phosphate; "triple stones")10%Infection stones; staghorn
Uric acid6–7%Radiolucent
Cystine1%Least common

Clinical presentation

  • Hematuria (a stone in the calyx or pelvis irritates the lining).
  • Renal colic: crampy pain from something being squeezed through a tube (ureter).
  • Obstruction → hydronephrosis → atrophy of the parenchyma. Sudden complete obstruction → acute renal failure; gradual obstruction → chronic renal failure.
  • Predisposition to infection.
Point to ponder: why do stones predispose to infection?A stone has no blood flow, so antibiotics cannot reach bacteria living in its nooks, crannies and spikes. The bacteria survive the antibiotic course and recur. (Obstruction also lets urine stagnate. beyond source)

4. Stone Types in Detail

Calcium oxalate / calcium phosphate (80%)

Metabolic causeApprox. share
Idiopathic hypercalciuria (increased calcium absorption or decreased renal reabsorption; blood calcium normal)50%
Hypercalcemia with hypercalciuria (e.g., hyperparathyroidism)10%
Hyperoxaluria5%
Hyperuricosuria (uric acid causes calcium to precipitate)20%
No known metabolic abnormality15–20%
  • High (alkaline) pH favors calcium phosphate stones. Dr. Kemp could not find a firm pH requirement for calcium oxalate.
  • By the numbers, calcium oxalate is the most likely stone in any patient.

Uric acid

  • Causes: gout and states of rapid cell turnover (leukemia, lymphoma; tumor lysis) → hyperuricemia and hyperuricosuria.
  • Low pH (acidic urine, below 5.0) favors formation. Hyperuricemia is not required.
  • Radiolucent on x-ray (the only one). Some contain calcium, which makes them partly visible.

Struvite (magnesium-ammonium-phosphate, "triple stones")

  • Form in alkaline urine with urinary tract infection (UTI) by urease-splitting bacteria: Proteus (the classic), also Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Citrobacter, Klebsiella pneumoniae. Urease splits urea → ammonia, which alkalinizes the urine. beyond source
  • Staghorn calculi: branch through the renal pelvis and calyces like deer or elk antlers.
  • Complication: xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (kidney parenchyma replaced by pale lipid-filled macrophages; "xantho" = yellow).
  • Why surgery (nephrectomy) can be needed: the stone branches throughout the pelvis and calyces, so it fills the whole system. You cannot pass it, and even lithotripsy is unlikely to break it up enough, so removing the kidney removes the stone.

Cystine

  • Cause: cystinuria (inherited, types I–III). Acidic urine. Radio-opaque, but less than the calcium and struvite stones.
Slide: stone type vs x-ray finding vs urine pH that promotes formation.
StoneX-rayUrine pH
Calcium oxalate / phosphateRadio-opaqueCalcium phosphate needs alkaline
Uric acidRadio-lucentAcidic (below 5.0)
StruviteRadio-opaqueAlkaline
CystineRadio-opaque (less)Acidic

Gross specimens

Slide: stone in a calyx (arrow); dilated pelvis (asterisk) with thinning of the parenchyma and fat filling the hilum.
Slide: stones in the calyceal system (yellow arrows); the blunted calyx at the end shows focal hydronephrosis.
Slide: a stone passed by a coworker, spiky, "like a mace." It shows why stones cause hematuria and pain.
Slide (autopsy): a hugely dilated kidney that looked like a pelvic mass. It is not autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (which can itself predispose to stones) but extensive hydronephrosis from a probable staghorn calculus.
Slide: staghorn calculus. Yellow arrows = stone fragments; blue arrow = residual renal parenchyma; black arrow = cloudy, infected urine (stones predispose to pyelonephritis).
Slide: xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Dilated calyces holding stone material; pale, macrophage-filled parenchyma.
Slide: a staghorn calculus removed whole. The branching pattern follows the pelvis and calyces.

5. Diseases Associated with Stones and Laboratory Evaluation

Diseases associated with nephrolithiasis

MechanismConditions
HypercalciuriaHyperparathyroidism; vitamin D excess; distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis; ketogenic diet
HyperuricosuriaGout; lymphoproliferative and myeloproliferative disorders (cell breakdown releases purines and pyrimidines → uric acid); tumor lysis syndrome; Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
HyperoxaluriaInflammatory bowel disease; small bowel resection
CystinuriaInherited; types I–III

Laboratory testing

  • Best: analyze the stone itself.
  • Urinalysis crystals: beware, crystals do not prove stones. Two characteristic shapes:
    • Envelope = calcium oxalate
    • Coffin lid = magnesium-ammonium-phosphate (struvite)
  • Urine pH: acidic → uric acid or cystine; alkaline → struvite or calcium phosphate. pH can point to the type.
Slide question42-year-old man, severe back pain and hematuria, radio-opaque mass at the left kidney. Uric acid is radiolucent, so out. Struvite and cystine are less common (cystine rarest). Hemosiderin is a pigment, not a stone. By the numbers, calcium oxalate.

6. Hydronephrosis

  • Basic description: dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces with atrophy of the overlying parenchyma (pressure of the trapped fluid thins the cortex).
  • Obstruction is the main cause, and stones are a common cause of obstruction.
Slide: normal kidney (left) vs hydronephrosis (right). The pelvis and calyces take up most of the cut surface and the cortex is thin.
CategoryCauses
CongenitalAberrant renal artery compressing the ureter; ureteral atresia; ureteral valve
Acquired: obstructing bodyCalculus; necrotic papilla (sloughs down the ureter)
Acquired: proliferative lesionPapilloma; tumor; benign prostatic hyperplasia (bladder fills and backs up, giving bilateral hydronephrosis)
Acquired: inflammatoryRetroperitoneal fibrosis (associated with IgG4 disease); prostatitis
NeurogenicSpinal cord injury (cannot empty the bladder; over time it backs up)
PregnancyUterus pinches the ureter
Dr. Kemp's tipThink general anatomy: what could a mass push on in this area? That gets you most of the causes.

TopicKey points
AKI categoriesPre-renal / renal (glomerular, tubulointerstitial, vascular) / post-renal
ATN castsMuddy brown granular and tubular epithelial cellular casts
WBC castsPyelonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis
RBC castsGlomerular injury (nephritic, rapidly progressive)
ATN causesIschemia or nephrotoxin (gentamicin, contrast, heavy metals, solvents, ethylene glycol)
Ethylene glycolAlcohol dehydrogenase → oxalic acid; oxalate crystals in kidney (polarize)
Tubule vulnerabilityHigh ATP need; concentrated luminal solutes
Stone frequenciesCa oxalate/phosphate 80%; struvite 10%; uric acid 6–7%; cystine 1%
Uric acid stoneRadiolucent; acidic urine; gout, leukemia, tumor lysis, Lesch-Nyhan
StruviteAlkaline urine; urease-splitting bacteria (Proteus); staghorn; coffin lids; xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis; may need nephrectomy
CystineCystinuria; acidic; less opaque
Calcium oxalateEnvelope crystals; most common; idiopathic hypercalciuria (50%)
HydronephrosisDilated pelvis and calyces; cortical atrophy; obstruction (stones, BPH, tumor, retroperitoneal fibrosis, pregnancy)
